articles.summary: 70-year-old Republican senator from Indiana Ron Alting announced his resignation after he was spotted multipl times at several Walmart stores shoplifting.
articles.body: 70-year-old Republican senator from Indiana Ron Alting announced his resignation after he was spotted multipl times at several Walmart stores shoplifting. His embarrassing shoplifting incidents were reported in Lafayette, Monticello and Florida. In a Facebook post Wednesday afternoon, he wrote, "Twenty-eight years ago, I asked the people of this community for the privilege of representing them in the Indiana Senate. It has been the greatest honor of my life."Addressing the shoplifting incidents, he wrote: "Over the past several weeks, I have been undergoing extensive medical evaluation for concerning changes in my judgment, behavior and cognitive functioning. That evaluation has included specialists in neurology, geriatrics and mental health, as well as an MRI and other testing. That work is continuing as my doctors seek a definitive diagnosis.""After many difficult conversations with my family, my doctors and people I have trusted for many years, I have concluded that I need to bring my time in public office to an end and devote my attention to my health and my family."But voting in this year's election is already underway and his name is there on the ballot. Alting said if he's elected, his successor will be chosen through the Republican Party's vacancy process. "I have great confidence that this process will produce an outstanding leader who will serve Senate District 22 and its people well," he wrote.What are the shoplifting incidents?Alting has not been charged in the Indiana incidents, according to court records. Elkhart County Prosecutor Vicki Becker has been asked to investigate several reported cases in two Lafayette Walmarts.Monticello police have not responded with the "factual circumstances" of the Oct. 1 shoplifting, as required by Indiana open record laws.“I was shocked when everything developed the last two weeks,” said Tracy Brown, chairman of the Tippecanoe County Republican party, noting he knew Alting’s resignation might be a possibility. “I understand the direction he is taking.”Journal and Courier reported that Alting consulted with Dr Greg Loomis, former Tippecanoe County health department director and a retired neurologist, who said Wednesday that Alting's most recent MRI scan shows typical clusters of cholesterol pieces that are common for someone who is 70 and has some health challenges. “There was no evidence of anything suggestive of a neurodegenerative disorder like Alzheimer’s disease. articles.title: Outposts, violence, impunity: The anatomy of Israeli settler land grabs
articles.summary: With government backing and little accountability, an ominous pattern casts a shadow over the Palestinian olive harvest.
articles.body:
Beita, occupied West Bank – Olive harvest season is traditionally a time when Palestinian families gather in their groves, pick olives and cook over open fires.

But when Musa Bani Shamsa and his 17-year-old son, who requested anonymity, arrived at his land in Beita, southeast of Nablus, the groves were empty.

On the morning of October 14 after they arrived, a group of masked Israeli men surrounded them. They carried pistols, knives, pipes, sticks and a hammer, Shamsa told Al Jazeera. Only their eyes were visible.

“At one point, I would take the beating for my son, and at another, my son would take the beating for me,” he said. “I was afraid they would kill him, kill him dead, because this has happened a lot.”

He lifted his shirt to show his bruises and stab wounds that were still healing. The beating lasted at least 20 minutes until he and his son were left lying on the ground. Shamsa was bleeding and lost consciousness.

“They thought we were dead, so they left us,” he said.

Shamsa said his attackers came from an Israeli outpost on the adjacent hill. Three days after the assault, his son was still unable to speak from the shock.

Settler violence across the occupied West Bank is rising sharply.

Since September 1, the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs recorded more than 200 attacks on Palestinian farmers, more than the total number of similar assaults for the entire season last year.

With more beatings, arson attacks and livestock theft, “people are afraid,” Shamsa said, “in every sense of the word.”

He shares that fear but refuses to abandon his land.

Harvesting begins earlier, at 5am. People block roads with stones to slow approaching settlers and take turns picking olives and keeping watch from rooftops with binoculars.

When settlers approach, families flee. Some return at night to harvest by phone light.

But these precautions offer little protection. In nearby villages, Shamsa said, settlers wait until farmers have finished picking before stealing their harvest and equipment.

“They come and take their olives and beat them, and they also take the mats they place under the olive trees,” he said. “Every time we give up a little, they take a little more. They do not want to give us safety.”

At the centre of Israeli settlement expansion are outposts, which often begin with little more than a flag, a tent or a livestock pen on Palestinian land. Established near Palestinian villages, they can expand to control surrounding fields and grazing areas.

From his porch, Khalil Tafakji, a cartographer and an expert on borders and settlements, pointed to a hill where Israeli flags flew above Palestinian homes.

He described outposts as “the offspring of the mother settlements”.

Positioned between existing Israeli settlements, they help link them and extend Israeli control “over the largest possible area of land with the smallest number of residents”, Tafakji told Al Jazeera.

Under international law, all Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank are illegal. Outposts are also illegal under Israeli law until approved by the government, yet many receive state support even before formal recognition.

“The state is behind the settlers, supporting them financially, morally, politically, militarily and in every detail,” Tafakji said.

In 2024, settlers established 62 new outposts, backed by 75 million shekels ($20m) in government funding. In total, the government has channelled at least 100 million shekels ($30m) to outposts and farms for security equipment and infrastructure, including roads, vehicles, drones, cameras and electric gates, according to Peace Now, an Israeli NGO. The government also retroactively legalises outposts.

In March, Israel’s security cabinet approved 34 new settlements , including 10 existing outposts. Israeli media reported that the decision provides for water and electricity infrastructure before final planning approval.

In Beita, a similar pattern is unfolding. Israel authorised the Evyatar outpost, first established in 2013, as a settlement in 2024. Since then, residents said, three smaller outposts have emerged around it.

Rabee al-Sharafa, a Beita resident living on the edge of the village, said settlers at first draw power from lines near the village before infrastructure is formally extended to them.

“If there is a power line close to the village, they may simply steal from it, no problem,” he said. “If it is cut off from them, they have no problem. The electricity company comes and extends it to them.”

As the number of outposts rises, so too do the threats of violence and force to remove Palestinian families from their land.

“The policy they follow is a policy of slow surrender,” al-Sharafa said of the settlers.

In March, 10 masked men armed with sticks, machetes and axes attacked a family and threatened to kill its members if they did not leave, he said. The family fled. Another home was emptied in June, and since early October, settlers have targeted a third, cutting off its electricity and water.

“We compare it to a string of prayer beads that comes apart,” al-Sharafa said.

The Israeli army protects the settlers, and Palestinians are rarely able to get recourse through the legal system .

When residents try to defend their homes, settlers “immediately bring the army against you”, al-Sharafa said. “Sometimes the army knows there is an attack but does not want to intervene until the attack is over.”

Al Jazeera has reached out to the Israeli military for comment but has yet to receive a response.

The law is also used to take the land itself.

Israel draws on a patchwork of Ottoman, British and Jordanian laws alongside its own military orders to seize Palestinian territory. Under an Ottoman-era law, land left uncultivated for several years can be claimed by the state. Israel uses this provision to declare areas “state land”, where Tafakji said many settlements have been established.

Other land is seized through military orders or expropriated for “public purposes”.

“They are confiscating our lands in order to establish another state and expel us. This is a process of uprooting and replacement,” Tafakji said.

Palestinians with formal title deeds have occasionally won in Israeli courts. But even then, “the military governor comes and turns it into a military zone,” Tafakji said.

In Beita, Shamsa fears that if violence forces farmers to abandon their olive groves, Israel could eventually claim them as state property.

He kept a tent on his land for about six years to enjoy time with friends and family, but settlers demolished it.

“If I abandon [the land] for a few years, they could cut down the trees and use that to say the land belongs to the state,” he said.

Meanwhile, criminal complaints rarely lead anywhere. Of the police investigations into settler violence monitored by the Israeli rights group Yesh Din from 2005 to 2023, 94 percent were closed without an indictment .

“Who are we supposed to complain to? Complain to the one oppressing you?” Shamsa asked.

articles.title: How Sudan’s shift to drone warfare is fuelling a civilian crisis
articles.summary: Drone attacks on supply lines and safe cities are taking a devastating toll on civilians.
articles.body:
In the Imtidad Nasser neighbourhood east of Sudan’s capital Khartoum, residents are grappling with a terrifying new reality of skies filled with drones.

“We heard the buzz of drones in the sky, but did not pay attention to it at first,” Ahmed Abdel Hamid, a resident of the area, told Al Jazeera about a recent drone attack by the Rapid Support Forces (RSF).

Then, anti-aircraft fire and two huge explosions shook the area, killing three children from a family in the community.

A devastating wave of drone attacks across Sudan has killed more than 160 people in recent days, marking a lethal evolution in the conflict between competing military forces which began in April 2023.

A rise in the use of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) by the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the paramilitary RSF has pushed the war deep into residential neighbourhoods, driven by shifting battlefield motives and a mutual desire to exhaust the opponent.

The use of drones is a relatively new development in the brutal civil war, which is now in its fourth year and has killed at least 59,000 people, according to conflict monitor ACLED. Some 14 million people have been displaced from their homes, with 4.5 million fleeing the country.

In the meantime, the SAF and the RSF have continued to vie for control of different parts of the country, mostly through ground invasions and fighting – and often at the cost of civilians. The massacre in el-Fasher in the west of the country last year – described by Amnesty International as “ ethnic cleansing ” – propelled the crisis to international headlines. RSF fighters murdered tens of thousands of inhabitants of the city after holding it under siege for 18 months and then capturing it – at the time the last SAF stronghold in the Darfur region.

Now, the intensified reliance on drones by both sides reflects a deliberate shift towards long-range, preemptive operations. For the SAF, drones offer a crucial tool to navigate complex geography and neutralise RSF advantages.

Military expert Abu Bakr Abdel Rahim said the army’s main motive for escalating drone strikes deep inside the Darfur and Kordofan regions is “targeting command and control centres, fuel and ammunition depots, and main supply routes, especially those linked to the borders with Libya, Chad and South Sudan”.

Geography plays a pivotal role in this strategy. “The Darfur region is vast, separated from the army’s current concentration areas in Kordofan by desert distances and long, militarily exposed roads, making ground advance highly complex without massive engineering, aerial, and logistical cover,” Abdel Rahim explained.

Through these targeted strikes, Abdel Rahim noted, army leadership seeks to weaken the RSF’s “ability to assemble its forces and launch counterattacks, or reclaim the strategic areas it lost”. Furthermore, by striking cities like Nyala , the army aims to “strike their morale, make them feel insecure even in their rear control areas, and disrupt any efforts to establish parallel administrative entities”.

Military officials say there are specific tactical goals behind the recent escalation. Mohamed Didan, spokesperson for the SAF’s Special Action Forces in Kordofan, stated in a Facebook post that the army launched “75 air strikes targeting fixed and moving targets, along with infantry forces, vehicles, commanders and individuals from the Rapid Support Forces” across Kordofan, West Darfur and South Darfur.

Didan directly linked the RSF’s recent drone attacks on Khartoum to their battlefield losses, attributing the escalation to “the killing of about 80 mobilised personnel for the forces in strikes that targeted them in the Al-Dabbab area in West Kordofan”.

He added that the RSF is deliberately targeting civilian infrastructure, “as happened at Khartoum airport, fuel stations in Damazin, and the electrical transformer station in Tendelti city in North Kordofan state last Tuesday, which led to the blackout of cities in the state and the neighbouring North Kordofan state”.

In response, the RSF issued a statement on Monday accusing the military of using drones to carry out “massacres in the livestock market in Nyala and al-Na’am market in Abyei, and at a truck station in the al-Dabbab area in West Kordofan “.

A Sudanese government official, speaking to Al Jazeera on condition of anonymity, said the military’s use of drones is strictly tactical. “The army does not target civilians, but it considers all military and logistical sites and supply lines of the Rapid Support Forces as legitimate targets,” the official stated.

Civilians are paying the highest price for all this. The deadliest recent attack occurred near a market in al-Dabba town in West Kordofan, where a drone struck a transport hub, killing 80 people.

Early on Monday, an army drone attack hit the RSF stronghold of Nyala, killing 17 people, while a strike by the paramilitary group on a gathering of displaced people in the Blue Nile province killed 41 individuals.

The United Nations has condemned the strikes. “We are alarmed by the continued deadly drone strikes across the country that are killing civilians, including children, and that are disrupting central services,” Stephane Dujarric, spokesperson for the UN secretary-general, told reporters.

An investigative report by the Centre for Information Resilience (CIR) revealed that 21 different drone models have been used since the war erupted.

A diverse international supply chain is behind their procurement of these weapons, which have been found to originate mainly from six countries: Belarus, Iran, China, Russia, Sudan and Turkiye.

According to the CIR investigation, the RSF has deployed 10 different types of drones, while the SAF has used five different models. The overall result is a terrifying and rapidly mechanising conflict where the skies offer no sanctuary to the civilians below.

articles.title: BrahMos goes global, eyes next-gen missile by 2028; 1,500-km strike variant on radar
articles.summary: BrahMos Aerospace is expanding its missile development and export ambitions, with a prototype of its next-generation BrahMos-NG system targeted for
articles.body: BrahMos Aerospace is expanding its missile development and export ambitions, with a prototype of its next-generation BrahMos-NG system targeted for 2027-28 and a 1,500-km-range variant on its longer-term roadmap. The company is accelerating research and development, strengthening its supply chain and engaging foreign militaries interested in air-launched versions of the supersonic cruise missile, CEO and managing director Dr Jaiteerth Joshi said in an interview with ANI on Thursday.BrahMos-NG is being developed as a smaller, lighter and stealthier version of the existing missile. It will feature higher indigenous content, new technologies and advanced materials. The system is being developed jointly by India's Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO) and Russia's NPO Mashinostroyeniya through BrahMos Aerospace.The company plans to develop the first prototype by 2027 or 2028. The missile will initially be developed in an airborne configuration, potentially expanding India's air-launched strike capabilities.Foreign militaries show interest in air-launched BrahMosBrahMos Aerospace is in talks with foreign countries interested in integrating the air-launched missile into their air forces. Some of these countries operate the Sukhoi-30 fighter aircraft, which is also used by the Indian Air Force.Interest is also emerging in BrahMos-NG, with potential customers looking at the next-generation system ahead of its development. The company is engaging with interested parties on the missile's capabilities and possible integration.The growing interest follows BrahMos' combat deployment during Operation Sindoor in May 2025, when the Indian Armed Forces used the weapon system in active warfare for the first time.The missile was deployed against critical targets, including major Pakistani airbases such as Nur Khan. Its combat performance has drawn greater attention from foreign militaries seeking weapons that can adapt to rapidly evolving battlefield conditions.BrahMos Aerospace CEO Dr Jaiteerth Joshi said the missile had demonstrated its ability to engage targets accurately in real time. He said no BrahMos missile was intercepted during the combat operation.1,500-km-range variant remains at conceptual stageBrahMos Aerospace is also exploring a major extension of the missile's strike range to 1,500 km. The proposed variant remains at the conceptual stage, with the company discussing further upgrades with its Russian joint venture partner.The range-extension programme is being pursued in phases. According to Joshi, test firings from land, sea and air have validated longer-range capabilities beyond the missile's original 290-km strike range.The proposed 1,500-km variant would mark a significant expansion of the missile's planned reach. However, the company has not announced a development or deployment timeline for it.Production expansion targets rising demandBrahMos Aerospace is prioritising the completion of existing orders from the Indian Armed Forces while preparing to meet growing demand from domestic and international customers.Its production units in Hyderabad, Nagpur, Pilani and Lucknow are working towards fulfilling the pending orders. The company also plans to accelerate research and development by establishing 'Tech-bricks' for specialised technologies required to develop and test future BrahMos systems.A key part of the expansion plan is to strengthen the supply chain and increase production capacity in case of emergencies or a sudden surge in demand.The company intends to expand the number of suppliers for individual systems and sub-systems from the earlier one or two industry partners to as many as 45 sources. The move is expected to widen the supplier base and encourage competition on quality and pricing.Combat record strengthens export prospectsBrahMos has become a key component of India's defence export strategy, with its operational performance adding to its international profile. The company secured its first export order in 2022, before the missile's combat deployment, and subsequently signed an export deal with the Philippines.BrahMos Aerospace has since signed deals with two more Southeast Asian countries this year. Orders and deliveries involving the Philippines, Indonesia and Vietnam are expected to take the missile's exports beyond $600 million.The missile's export prospects are part of a broader expansion in India's defence exports, which have reached Rs 38,400 crore, registering annual growth of 62.7%.The system is increasingly being positioned as a flagship of India's defence manufacturing capabilities and push for self-reliance. Its combat performance during Operation Sindoor has also strengthened its profile among foreign military buyers.Navy contract reinforces domestic manufacturingOn October 6, the Ministry of Defence signed a contract with BrahMos Aerospace for the procurement of fire control systems and launchers for Indian Navy ships.The contract has a minimum indigenous content requirement of 68% and is expected to encourage participation from Indian industries, including micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs).The project adds to BrahMos Aerospace's domestic production commitments as it pursues new missile variants, expands its supplier network and seeks to strengthen its position in the international defence market.

articles.title: Stephen Hubbard returns to US after years in Russian prison
articles.summary: American Stephen Hubbard has returned to the U.S. after being detained in Russia for nearly four years. The freed American arrived at Lackland Air Force Base in San Antonio early Thursday morning. Russia had accused Hubbard, who lived in Ukraine at the time, of fighting on behalf of Ukraine after Russia launched its war. Former…
articles.body:
American Stephen Hubbard has returned to the U.S. after being detained in Russia for nearly four years. The freed American arrived at Lackland Air Force Base in San Antonio early Thursday morning.

Russia had accused Hubbard, who lived in Ukraine at the time, of fighting on behalf of Ukraine after Russia launched its war. Former President Biden’s administration had designated Hubbard as wrongfully detained.

President Trump said he personally asked Russian President Vladimir Putin to release Hubbard in a phone call, and special envoy Steve Witkoff traveled to Russia to secure his release.

“It was my honor to be with Stephen in St. Petersburg today before he departed for the United States,” Witkoff wrote in a post to the social platform X. “President Trump called Stephen to check on him and reaffirm his unwavering commitment to bringing all Americans wrongfully detained home.”

Hubbard’s release was secured without an exchange.

The State Department shared a photo to X on Wednesday showing Hubbard surrounded by family holding an American flag as he reentered the U.S.

“Stephen is finally back in America with his loved ones after enduring four years of unjust detention,” the department wrote. “Our nation celebrates his return and offers him our prayers as he begins this next chapter of his life.”

The release comes as Trump faces political backlash at home for taking a friendlier stance toward Putin and backing away from Ukraine. The president signed an executive order waiving sanctions on Russian energy and announced a deal with Putin to purchase hundreds of thousands of tons of Russian diesel, aiming to bring down costs for Americans.

Witkoff visited Russia both to secure Hubbard’s release and to push for a deal to end the war between Russia and Ukraine. The special envoy drew backlash from members of both parties for calling Putin a “humanitarian” in the meeting.

“You talk so much about my president, President Trump, being a humanitarian,” Witkoff said to Putin. “You are a humanitarian also, sir, and I salute that.”

Multiple Republicans, including Sen. Thom Tillis (N.C.), criticized Witkoff’s comments on social media .

“You should go back to Ukraine and ask the families of the children Putin has kidnapped and murdered whether they agree your friend Putin is a ‘humanitarian,’” Tillis wrote on X .

articles.title: France reports first human case of livestock virus Shamonda after patient dies
articles.summary: France on Thursday reported the first human case of the Shamonda virus usually found in livestock in a patient who later died, with authorities adding there was no risk to the general population at this stage.
articles.body: France on Thursday reported the first human case of the Shamonda virus usually found in livestock in a patient who later died, with authorities adding there was no risk to the general population at this stage. It is suspected that the victim was bitten by a midge carrying the virus in eastern France where it had circulated among animals this spring and summer, the government said in a statement. The Stockholm-based European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control said it was monitoring the situation. “ECDC is in contact with the French authorities and European partners to investigate the potential public health implications,” it said in a statement. The patient died in early October and had been receiving treatment for a serious illness that made them more susceptible to infection than the general population, the ECDC said. “Investigations into whether the virus caused or contributed to the patient’s death and how the infection was acquired are ongoing,” it said. Virus spreading in animals in Europe The victim was a man in 60s living in the Lyon area in eastern France, local newspaper Le Progres reported. “Based on the knowledge available regarding this virus, no health risk to the general population has been identified to date,” the government said. Shamonda is transmitted by biting midges and most commonly found in cattle, though it has also been found in horses, alpaca, sheep and goats, according to the World Organisation for Animal Health (WOAH). It is not classified as a disease under the EU Animal Health Law and not subject to official surveillance or control measures. Identified in Nigeria in the mid-1960s, Shamonda was first confirmed in Europe in late July after genomic tests on sick cattle in southern Germany, Switzerland and eastern France. France’s weekly animal health surveillance bulletin said the virus had also been detected in Austria, Belgium, Ireland, Italy, Liechtenstein, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Portugal, Slovenia, Spain, and the UK’s Jersey. The virus has several effects on animals. A study of nine French dairy farms found milk production fell by up to 75%, with affected cattle showing diarrhoea, weakness, loss of appetite and, less often, fever, French animal health authorities said.

articles.title: Nothing personal between me and Trump, Zelensky tells CNN
articles.summary: After a bitter rift with Donald Trump left many in Ukraine fearing that the US president had swung behind Russia again, President Volodymyr Zelensky addressed the dispute head on: there’s nothing personal between me and Trump, he told CNN, but cozying up to Vladimir Putin would only “make him stronger.”
articles.body: After a bitter rift with Donald Trump left many in Ukraine fearing that the US president had swung behind Russia again, President Volodymyr Zelensky addressed the dispute head on: there’s nothing personal between me and Trump, he told CNN, but cozying up to Vladimir Putin would only “make him stronger.” Ties between the US and Ukraine have badly deteriorated in recent weeks. Zelensky said Trump was “on the wrong side of history” after he announced a deal to buy Russian fuel, upending international efforts to isolate Russia. Trump then waived some sanctions against Russia, drawing criticism even from his own party. Ukraine’s forces found their access to the Elon Musk-run Starlink service restricted. Speaking to CNN from Kyiv on Thursday, Zelensky took a conciliatory tone, saying the tensions were “not about personalities” – but warned that Putin had no intention of stopping the war. “My attitude to Putin is very clear. I think that if we lift sanctions, we will make him stronger. It’s not something personal between me and President Trump, and of course I’m against of any lifting of sanctions.” Zelensky spoke to CNN amid a renewed diplomatic push from Trump’s envoys to find a resolution to the four-and-a-half-year conflict. On Wednesday, US special envoy Steve Witkoff spent three hours talking to Russian President Vladimir Putin in St. Petersburg, controversially describing him as a “humanitarian” for his decision to release 74-year-old American prisoner Stephen Hubbard. Witkoff had met with Zelensky in Norway a day earlier. Trump insisted on Wednesday that tightening sanctions on Russia would have meant Hubbard stayed imprisoned. “You could forget about him, you’d never see him again, he’d be back in jail for 25 years,” he said in response to a question from CNN’s Kaitlin Collins. He added that tighter sanctions would imperil the chances of a deal over Ukraine: “When you’re close to a deal and you have delicate negotiations, you don’t put sanctions on.” Putin ‘plays’ with lives Zelensky said his meeting in Norway’s capital Oslo was productive, but that he wasn’t convinced of Putin’s commitment to peace. Following the visit from Witkoff Putin agreed to talks in November while giving few firm details. “Putin is playing, you know, he is a player,” Zelensky said. “It’s a pity because he plays with the lives of other people, and of course he doesn’t want (to stop the war). So what we want from our partners (is) not to give him a possibility to be stronger and break us.” Trump said on Wednesday his administration is “the closest we’ve been” to settling the war in Ukraine – only for Russia to launch hundreds of drones and ballistic missiles against its neighbor overnight. So far, Putin has also maintained his maximalist demands from Ukraine – including territory. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio told reporters on Wednesday that “the fight now is really concentrated on what happens in the remainder of Donbas,” the eastern Ukrainian region that is mostly under Russian control. He said “there’s been some creative ideas that have been put out there about how to resolve that difference.” Freeze the front lines? Speaking to CNN, Zelensky alluded to the possibility of freezing the current frontlines in order to “ceasefire, stop the killing, sit and speak.” However, he made it clear the idea of Ukraine giving up territory currently under its control to Russia is a non-starter, and Kyiv would never recognize occupied areas as part of Russia. “Our land is very important because it’s about people. It’s not about kilometers,” he said. “A lot of people died defending this land, defending our independence, our country.” “Nobody will recognize these territories, which are temporarily occupied, as Russian territories, and I think Russia understands it. It’s a pity if somebody doesn’t understand, but it’s up to them,” the Ukrainian president added. There have been some signs of tensions easing after Kyiv accused the US of limiting intelligence sharing on incoming Russian missiles, slowing down vital Starlink services and delaying weapon supplies. Zelensky said earlier this week that intelligence sharing has been restored, but he told CNN Starshield, SpaceX’s military-grade service is not yet fully restored. But Ukraine’s critical shortage of interceptor missiles means that even though its military now gets a warning of an incoming Russian ballistic missile, it has nothing to shoot it down with. Zelensky also told CNN Thursday that while Ukraine’s European allies have provided some air defense missiles to Ukraine, “it’s not enough to defend ourselves.” Ukraine, Zelensky said, now mostly needs two things from its allies: “Not to lift sanctions from Putin … (and) to give us better missiles.”

"Now, we have dangerous days ahead of the elections," Zelenskyy said on Sunday, referring to the Nov. 3 midterms in the US. Photographer: Olga Ivashchenko/Bloomberg via Getty Images

articles.title: Why Serbian elections are so important - as students challenge 12 years of Vučić rule
articles.summary: After two years of student protests, Serbians vote on Sunday in elections that could bring down the ruling party.
articles.body:
Rallies have been taking place across Serbia on Thursday, the final day of campaigning ahead of a snap election billed as a referendum on the country's future.

After two years of student protests, Serbians vote for a new parliament on Sunday in elections that threaten populist leader Aleksandar Vučić's 12 years in power.

The main threat to Vučić's dominance in Serbian politics comes from a two-year-old student movement, but there are concerns surrounding the fairness of the vote.

Why is this student movement so important?

They have no obvious leaders and are not used to politics, but the "Student List-Students Win" movement has attracted anti-government voters across Serbia.

The Student List is fielding candidates from across Serbian society - and as he joined students marching towards Belgrade, lead candidate and cardiologist Ilija Srdanović said history was being rewritten: "The energy is unstoppable."

It all began on 1 November 2024, when the concrete canopy collapsed outside Novi Sad train station, in Serbia's second biggest city, killing 16 people.

The tragedy was seen as emblematic of corruption and negligence in Serbia. Critics linked the station's fatally flawed renovation to a president who had closely associated himself with the project.

What started as weekly student protests demanding justice on university campuses and city streets soon became a national movement, often at a local level, that encompassed far more sections of Serbian society, including farmers, actors and judges.

The Serbian Progressive party (SNS), founded by Vučić, was shaken and within weeks the prime minister resigned. Belgrade saw one of its biggest ever protests in March 2025, and while the leaderless student movement increased in strength, they organised themselves through student assemblies or plenums.

At the last election in 2023, Vučić's SNS was challenged by a loose coalition of pro-EU parties, that later fell apart. This time he faces a far clearer threat from a student movement that has shunned the mainstream opposition parties.

Anger lingers in Serbia after train station tragedy

Vučić has spent two terms as president and cannot seek a third term, so he is now leading his party with the aim of returning to the post of prime minister, which he left in 2017 .

The right-wing populist leader has doubled down on unfounded allegations that his opponents are not so much students and professors, but "mighty great powers" seeking to overthrow Serbia. And he has vowed an end to what he sees as the politicisation of schools and universities.

Vučić has steered a careful path with the West, continuing to back Serbia's candidacy for the European Union, while refusing to impose sanctions on Russia for its full-scale war in Ukraine. Several government ministers attended the Belgrade funeral of war criminal Ratko Mladić, prompting EU anger at his "glorification".

Helena Ivanov of the Henry Jackson Society, a foreign policy think tank, says the students have been able to mobilise the masses in a way traditional opposition parties have not been able to - and this is Vučić's biggest challenge since he came to power.

"He's been running in all elections Serbia has had since the introduction of multi-party election system - so obviously defeating him isn't going to be easy, but this time around President Vučić isn't going to have an easy time either," she told the BBC from Belgrade.

Embattled Serbian president resigns, paving way for early elections

Serbia has a parliament with 250 seats and there is just one national constituency under proportional representation.

Voting runs from 07:00 (06:00 GMT) and ends at 20:00 on Sunday.

There are 6.45 million registered voters and anyone over the age of 18 gets the right to choose which party's list of candidates to vote for.

Sunday's vote involves 18 lists but only seven of them are fielding the full 250 candidates. MPs are elected according to how much support the list receives if it wins more than 3% of the vote.

Several opposition parties have pulled out in favour of the Student List.

Who are the student leaders and what do they stand for?

Far from being students themselves, the candidates are made up of teachers and university professors, actors and doctors, farmers and scientists.

They still have no leaders, but top candidate Ilija Srdanović is a cardiology professor in Novi Sad, while others include ex-basketball star Dejan Bodiroga, renowned actor Tihomir Stanić and former National Bank of Serbia governor Dejan Šoškić.

Under an 11-point programme , the student movement wants to:

eradicate corruption by forming a police unit to arrest those responsible for it

purge officials in the internal affairs ministry of anyone who broke rules on cracking down on protesters, or anyone linked to organised crime

reform Serbia's skewed media scene and free the public broadcaster of political control

stop recruiting party loyalists to head public enterprises

Vučić and the SNS party deny corruption and seeking to influence the media.

European observers are monitoring Sunday's vote, but even beforehand the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe (PACE) has spoken of a "tense and divisive electoral climate" and a "referendum-like atmosphere".

Serbia's election commission says elections are free and the ballot is secret. However, independent watchdog CRTA has warned of a campaign that has seen threats and physical violence , and opposition activists subjected to surveillance.

In a report ahead of the vote, it said instead of ensuring equal conditions for candidates, "a range of institutions, from ministries to local governments, became involved in electoral engineering".

Serbian media has seen almost three-quarters of TV coverage devoted to government representatives, the watchdog complained, and alleged that ministries and local governments had become caught up in "electoral engineering".

Some 160 attacks have been recorded on media and journalists in Serbia this year, says the European Centre for Press and Media Freedom.

articles.title: ‘Looksmaxxing’ influencer Clavicular pleads not guilty to Massachusetts rape charges
articles.summary: “Looksmaxxing” influencer Clavicular pleaded not guilty in Massachusetts court Thursday to criminal rape charges stemming from an alleged May 2025 incident at this family’s house in Cape Cod.
articles.body: “Looksmaxxing” influencer Clavicular pleaded not guilty in Massachusetts court Thursday to criminal rape charges stemming from an alleged May 2025 incident at this family’s house in Cape Cod. Clavicular, 20, whose real name is Braden Peters, was charged with rape, drugging someone for sexual intercourse and procuring liquor for someone under 21 years old, according to a criminal complaint filed on Sept. 8 in Orleans District Court in Barnstable County, Massachusetts. Aleksandra Vasilevna Mendoza, an 18-year-old influencer known online as Alorah or Alorah Ziva, alleged that last May, when she was 17 and in Massachusetts, Peters called her an Uber to his family’s home in Chatham, a beachfront town in Cape Cod. When Mendoza was at Peters’ home, she alleged, he got her drunk with vodka during a livestream on Twitch and then raped her while she was asleep, the criminal complaint from the Chatham Police Department said. At the time, his mother and grandmother were allegedly in the house. A representative and Peters’s lawyer declined to comment ahead of the arraignment. Mendoza’s lawyer also declined to comment. Peters has previously denied any wrongdoing and defended himself in a series of posts on X. At his Thursday arraignment, a judge set bail for Peters at $10,000 after his defense team filed a memo in Orleans District Court on Wednesday asking for “fair and reasonable bail” in that amount. In it, his attorney argued that Peters is neither a danger to the community nor a flight risk and pointed out that he has no history of felony criminal convictions. A court clerk confirmed Thursday that Peters paid the $10,000 bail in cash. The criminal charges follow a civil suit Mendoza filed in Miami last year in which she accused Peters of sexual battery in connection with the alleged May 2025 incident in Cape Cod. In the civil suit, she also alleged he injected her face with a non-FDA-approved fat-dissolving substance during a November livestream in Florida. A source familiar with the matter confirmed that the criminal charges against Peters stem from Mendoza’s allegations. Earlier this month, Mendoza refiled her civil lawsuit and dropped the sexual assault allegations against Peters. At the time, her lawyer said it was to avoid interfering with the criminal case in Massachusetts. The Wednesday memo from Peters’ team also lays out his defense, arguing that Mendoza willingly created social media content with Peters and previously described him to her followers as “so nice.” The memo also says she continued to hang out with Peters and profit from their relationship after the alleged Cape Cod incident in May 2025. The filing also includes a letter allegedly handwritten by Mendoza, in which she allegedly wrote, “Braden, you have my loyalty 100% ... I admire the man you are,” and added that she wanted to continue working with Peters. In screenshots of messages between Peters and Mendoza included in the filing, Mendoza appeared to imply she wanted to engage in a romantic relationship with Peters. By early 2026, Peters’ lawyer alleged, Mendoza’s brand deals were drying up as Peters’ success continued to grow. She then filed the civil suit, the filing said. When she reported the alleged rape to Chatham police in June 2026, she told officers she had not undergone a sexual assault forensic examination. She told police she told one friend about the alleged assault, then later changed her story and said she never told anyone about it, according to the memo. This is not Peters’ first run-in with the law. Peters and two other people were charged in Florida in April with shooting at an alligator. He and another person pleaded no contest to unlawfully discharging a firearm in public and were given six months of probation and ordered to serve 20 hours of community service, according to NBC South Florida. He was also hospitalized in April in Miami after a suspected overdose, according to his representative. If you or someone you know has been sexually assaulted, call the National Sexual Assault Hotline at 1-800-656-4673. The hotline, run by the Rape, Abuse, & Incest National Network (RAINN), can put you in contact with your local rape crisis center. You can also access RAINN’s online chat service at rainn.org/get-help.

articles.title: Police should not be scared to wade in to stop wrongdoing, says Kemi Badenoch
articles.summary: The Tory leader calls for more support for police officers and the public when they step in to help.
articles.body:
Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has criticised punishments for people who intervene to "do the right thing" in a speech at the Police Federation conference.

Telling delegates she was "not scared to wade in", she called for more support for members of the public as well as police officers who step in to stop wrongdoing.

Badenoch also criticised Labour for failing to send a minister to the conference for two years in a row.

The prime minister's official deputy spokeswoman rejected the claims, stating the police have the government's "full backing" and are benefitting from investment. The BBC has contacted the Home Office for comment on ministerial attendance at the police conference.

In a speech at the conference, Badenoch said: "Too often these days, we fail to recognise sacrifice and service.

"Whether it's hounding brave and elderly veterans through the courts, hounding police officers who try to do the right thing, or even ordinary members of the public who step in to help only to find that they're in trouble themselves.

"It's no wonder the people in this country are becoming too scared to wade in, too scared to do the right thing. Well, I am different. I am not scared to wade in, and I am not scared to back the police."

The Conservative leader listed police officers who have been killed in the line of duty, such as PCs Matthew Blades and Tom Clough who died in the Cleveland A66 crash, and PC Andrew Harper , killed investigating a quad bike theft.

She also attacked police being investigated following controversial cases, including the case of 24-year-old Chris Kaba , who was shot by Sgt Matthew Blake in 2022 after he tried to ram his way past police cars.

The police officer was put on trial for murder before being cleared, with Badenoch saying his "job was made harder because he didn't get the backing he deserved".

Badenoch also attacked Labour, saying: "I think it is telling that for two years in a row, the Labour Government has not sent anyone to address this conference – not the policing minister, not the Home Secretary.

"You are the ones who enforce the law. You are the ones who ensure there are consequences for bad behaviour. That's why, if we want law and order back in our country, back on our streets, we need to back the police."

Responding, the prime minister's official deputy spokeswoman said: "I would reject those claims.

"The police have the government's full backing and as you will have seen from various reports this morning, we are continuing to invest in our police and we are bringing forward reforms following the Bernard Hogan Howe report in due course."

The Home Office has been contacted for comment about ministerial attendance at the conference and whether the government is still planning to recruit 13,000 police officers.

articles.title: From the streets to the ballot box: Serbia’s students hope for election win
articles.summary: Young Serbians have built a system that poses a threat to President Aleksandar Vucic’s grip on power.
articles.body:
A student-led movement has emerged as the most serious challenger to the long rule of the Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) and its leader, Aleksandar Vucic , ahead of Sunday’s election.

Over the past two years, many citizens, teachers, professors and other experts have joined the students, a protest group that has evolved into a political movement: “Student List–Students Win” (Studentska lista–Studenti pobeđuju).

The catalyst came after the collapse of a concrete canopy at the renovated Novi Sad railway station on November 1, 2024. Sixteen people were killed in the tragedy, which triggered public outrage over alleged corruption and raised questions about construction safety, the quality of renovation work, and government oversight. Students who led protests have sought a fundamental overhaul of a system they deem rotten.

‘Serbia belongs to people, not to criminals’

Kosta Golubovic, a law student at the University of Novi Sad, has been involved since day one.

“Change is clearly necessary. The state must belong to its people, not to the mafia and criminals,” he told Al Jazeera.

“The way they treat the judiciary, the catastrophic conditions at the local level, mayors resorting to violence, dying villages – along with dubious privatisations, money laundering, the erosion of every single institution, police being replaced by thugs, and an education system vanishing before our eyes… these are some of the reasons why change is needed,” said Golubovic.

Demonstrations transformed into the biggest protest movement in Serbia in years, joined by tens of thousands.

The students have not called for the overthrow of Vucic. But their persistence created one of the biggest threats to the president’s long grip on power.

Vucic became prime minister in 2014. In 2017, he was elected president, a traditionally ceremonial role that he has bolstered by maintaining influence over his SNS party.

Opposition parties and rights watchdogs accuse Vucic and his SNS party of bribing voters, stifling media freedom, violence against opponents, and ties with organised crime.

Vucic and his allies deny these allegations. But Serbia’s rating on Transparency International’s global corruption index has worsened gradually in recent years.

“Vucic is clearly afraid of us – it’s obvious. He knows that, for the first time in 16 years, the SNS is no longer the most popular political option in the country,” Golubovic said.

The students’ efficiency is down in part to its structure.

The old student parliament at the University of Belgrade has been replaced with plenums – daily assemblies where each group votes on its course of action. Working groups focus on strategy, donations, and security. Universities in different cities coordinate so demands remain broadly aligned.

This is why the students say they do things differently. One rule is to be leaderless, making it harder for authorities to disrupt the protests. Also, demonstrations must be peaceful, and any debris has to be cleaned up. Third, all decisions must be made democratically during hour-long plenary sessions in their university faculties.

“Even though the authorities mobilised criminal groups against the students and citizens participating in the protests, the students have remained focused on their goal: to oust a government they view as authoritarian and deeply corrupt,” said Natasa Kandic, a Serbian peace activist, sociologist, and founder of the Humanitarian Law Center (HLC) in Belgrade.

“For the first time in Serbia, they have managed to lead protests entirely without violence,” she said. “The video clips we see daily represent a new culture – one defined by irony, laughter, and the deliberate disregard for primitivism and political depravity.”

State-affiliated media have maligned the students. Some Serbian authorities claimed that the group has no programme, and Vucic labelled them as “terrorists”. But their leaders, experts from different fields, claim that they have a plan.

The platform is officially titled the “Student Plan” and is divided into three sections. There are 11 points.

Ilija Srdanovic, a cardiologist and the lead candidate and ballot holder for the Student List, explained that the platform deliberately avoids setting fixed, precise deadlines for the proposed changes. He argued that such timelines can only be determined once contributors have gained insight into the “full current state of affairs”.

“[We plan] many things – too many to list – but the goal is to change the system,” said Srdanovic in a brief call to Al Jazeera.

During debates, the establishment of a special prosecutorial police unit, a law on the origin of assets, transitional justice and the renovation of rural medical clinics are some frequent themes.

Could this be implemented in the case of a victory? Kandic is sceptical.

“The student movement doesn’t possess a transformative potential – the capacity to drive social change, break with the past, and alter a political climate where convicted war criminals are celebrated, Kosovo is treated as part of Serbia, and politicians from neighboring countries are branded as enemies,” he said.

articles.title: A Texas man put just $12,000 down on a home with 10 acres, built a glamping retreat using the extra land and turned the property into a business grossing more than $100,000 a year while keeping his day job
articles.summary: A US real estate investor has built a successful outdoor hospitality business on the outskirts of Houston, Texas, after buying a 10-acre residential
articles.body: A US real estate investor has built a successful outdoor hospitality business on the outskirts of Houston, Texas, after buying a 10-acre residential property with an upfront payment of just $12,000 (£9,200). Garrett Brown has a full-time job and also teaches through the property education platform BiggerPockets. He used a strategy he calls "land hacking" to build Cameron Ranch Glamping. According to an industry report published by Modern Campground, the business now earns more than $100,000 a year in gross revenue, without Brown having to leave his main job. By choosing residential property instead of undeveloped rural land, Brown avoided the long process of installing utilities and dealing with complex local planning rules. These challenges often delay new outdoor accommodation projects.Land hacking strategyTo start the business, Brown bought a house on 10 acres of unrestricted land for $550,000. Instead of making a standard down payment, he negotiated concessions with the seller and secured the property with a down payment of just 2 per cent. The land already had utility connections, enough septic system capacity, and road access through the main house. This meant he avoided spending years trying to get infrastructure and approvals in place for undeveloped land. He added his first accommodation unit to the property, a geodome made by Pacific Domes, which cost about $13,000. After adding the costs of clearing the ground, connecting utilities, and building an access path, his total start-up costs came to around $32,000. In its second full year of operation, the single dome charged an average of $422 per night and had an 88 per cent occupancy rate. According to figures shared by Modern Campground, the unit earned $95,000 in gross revenue and made $60,000 in net profit after the mortgage payments for the entire property were covered.Expanding without upfront capitalAfter the first dome proved successful, Brown expanded the business through revenue-sharing deals. This allowed him to grow the site while reducing his financial risk. He reached an agreement with OOD, an Estonian modular construction company, to install a mirrored glass cabin worth $129,000 on the property. OOD provided the cabin without requiring Brown to pay anything upfront. In return, the company receives 30 per cent of the gross revenue from bookings. During its first year on the property, the mirrored cabin reached a 90 per cent occupancy rate and earned $115,000 in gross revenue. To attract guests, Brown avoided relying too much on third-party booking platforms such as Airbnb. Research by business platform Side Hustle Nation shows that around 80 per cent of Cameron Ranch Glamping's bookings now come directly through its own website. This direct traffic mainly comes from targeted social media marketing. One short video featuring a galvanized "cowboy pool" on the property went viral and attracted more than 20 million views online.Automated operations and staffingAlthough Brown runs a busy glamping business while keeping his full-time job, he manages daily operations using automated property management software. The business uses Lodgify to manage reservations in one place, PriceLabs to change nightly rates automatically based on local demand, and Turno to organize cleaning schedules and staff changeovers. According to Side Hustle Nation, Brown pays local cleaners more than the usual market rate. They also handle maintenance tasks, such as replacing propane tanks for guest fire pits and outdoor heaters. Speaking on an episode of the industry podcast MC Fireside Chats, Brown explained that expert help was important when dealing with local regulations. He worked with a local architect and chose building designs that came with engineering documents already approved for use. This helped him secure commercial permits in an area where officials were not familiar with glamping projects.Named in memoryThe property also has personal meaning for its founder. Brown named the business Cameron Ranch Glamping in memory of his late brother. The name reflects the brand's tagline, "disconnect to reconnect." Most guests are couples who book short weekend stays or visit to celebrate special occasions. They choose the site for its mix of private rural surroundings and high-end facilities. Brown has since shared his experience in a book called The Glamping Investor, published through BiggerPockets. The book covers five years of business data and offers advice on financing for people who want to start their own outdoor hospitality businesses.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Would a new president end Russia’s war on Ukraine?
articles.summary: Professor David A. Super argues that President Trump’s reversal of U.S. policy toward Ukraine and his demand for new elections violate the Ukrainian Constitution and ignore the reality of Russia’s existential threat to the nation.
articles.body:
President Trump has dramatically reversed U.S. policy toward Ukraine. Just weeks after signing the sweeping Russian sanctions legislation crafted by the late Republican Sen. Lindsay Graham (R-S.C), he cancelled those sanctions .

He also cancelled other sanctions that have been in place since Russia invaded in 2022, exceeding his legal authority . He announced a murky and likely only symbolic deal to buy Russian diesel fuel. Most critically, he stopped sharing intelligence about Russian launches of ballistic missiles against Ukrainian cities, resulting in scores of dead civilians who were struck before Ukraine could detect and issue warnings to seek cover.

Trump and Elon Musk deny responsibility, but they may have also partially blocked the operation of Starlink terminals on which the Ukrainian defense forces depend.

Much of this Trump has justified in terms of vaguely defined American national interests. In addition, he has insisted that these actions will somehow hasten the end of the war in Ukraine. In particular, he has called for Ukraine to hold new elections to replace President Volodymyr Zelensky. This last demand might seem plausible to Americans that have not been following this conflict or traveled to Ukraine. Having spent much of last month teaching at Ukrainian Catholic University, I can offer perspective on that claim.

Zelensky was elected in 2019 with 73 percent of the vote. He unseated the incumbent president, whom he criticized for being insufficiently aggressive in fighting corruption. Zelensky also argued that the incumbent’s acrimonious relationship with Russia could hamper the resolution of Russia’s occupation of large parts of eastern and southern Ukraine.

Ordinarily, Ukrainian presidents serve five-year terms. The Ukrainian constitution, however, prohibits elections under conditions of martial law , which has been in effect since Russia’s full-scale invasion on Feb. 24, 2022. So when Trump demands that Ukrainians hold new elections in the midst of the war, he is demanding that they violate their constitution.

While teaching in Ukraine, I met a great many Ukrainians, most unaffiliated with the university where I taught. Not surprisingly, I encountered a wide range of opinions on Zelensky and other prominent Ukrainian politicians. Even among Zelensky’s harshest critics, not a single person advocated holding elections now. The reasons are obvious.

In any elections held now, Ukraine has no effective means of enabling its millions of citizens living under Russian occupation to vote. It also would have difficulty securing full participation by the millions of Ukrainian refugees scattered across Europe and beyond. Ukrainians feel deep gratitude toward their defense forces and would want soldiers to participate, but conditions on the front lines would make a secret ballot impossible. The same is true for many Ukrainian civilians living near the frontlines.

An election also would be extraordinarily dangerous for the Ukrainian people. As Russia tries to terrorize Ukrainians into capitulating, its missiles have systematically targeted places where Ukrainian civilians congregate: supermarkets, popular restaurants, schools, playgrounds, and the like. It trains new drone operators by having them hunt Ukrainian civilians in Kherson , a large city across the Dnieper River from Russian-occupied territory. People waiting in line to vote would present too inviting a target for Russia.

Many Ukrainians regard Zelensky the way the British regarded Winston Churchill: a valuable wartime leader but not the person they want leading the country forward after the fighting ends. Churchill was overwhelmingly elected in 1940 and surely would have won any other elections during World War II, but he was voted out two months after Germany’s defeat. Holding an election now, which Zelensky would almost certainly win, would deprive Ukrainians of the chance to select a new leader after the war. Ukrainians who dislike Zelensky most are therefore the strongest opponents of wartime elections.

The basic premise of Trump’s claim, however, is fundamentally flawed. Zelensky is not the obstacle to Ukraine’s capitulation to Russia. The Ukrainian people are . If Zelensky, or any new president, were to accept the terms Trump is demanding, mass demonstrations would immediately drive them from office. And rightly so.

Russia does not want Ukraine’s land: it will stop at nothing short of Ukraine’s annihilation. Russia President Vladimir Putin and his propagandists have repeatedly insisted that Ukraine is an illegitimate country that has no right to exist. Drawing on centuries-old ethnic stereotypes , they have derided Ukrainians as inferior to Russians fit only to serve Russia. Russia’s 2022 invasion was not limited to the parts of Ukraine it now demands: it tried to seize the Ukrainian capital, Kyiv, and second-largest city, Kharkiv. Russia was very clear that it sought to end Ukraine as an independent country.

Any peace purchased by conceding Ukrainian land and people to Russia would only last long enough for Russia to rearm and prepare its next invasion. As a prerequisite for peace talks, Russia has demanded that Ukraine surrender large swaths of territory that Russia has been unable to win on the battlefield. Those talks would presumably bring further demands.

In particular, Russia demands that Ukraine surrender its strongest fortifications, making subsequent Russian invasions easier. This is an old tactic: The peace Germany secured from Neville Chamberlain in Munich required Czechoslovakia to surrender all its border defenses. Six months later, Germany conquered the remainder of the country rendered defenseless by this concession.

In 1994, the U.S. heavily pressured Ukrainians to surrender their nuclear weapons, promising that the U.S. would ensure the country’s territorial integrity. Had Ukraine kept its arsenal — the third-largest in the world — Russia would never have dared invade. When Russia attacked in 2014, Ukrainians quickly learned that America’s word was worthless. We would not even send them weapons. Instead, we pressured them to accept continued Russian occupation of large parts of their country as a price of peace.

This land-for-peace deal did not stop Russia from invading again in 2022. The Ukrainian people will not be fooled again, no matter who their president is.

Trump has already done immense damage to U.S. international credibility. His intelligence cut-off has cost many innocent Ukrainians their lives. His alleged throttling of Starlink terminals paid for by Ukraine and its European allies will wreck the U.S. arms industry’s international credibility.

Although much of this damage is irreparable, Trump should still walk back these imprudent actions immediately. The U.S. should always stand by western democracies, not murderous dictators.

David A. Super is Carmack Waterhouse Professor of Law and Economics at Georgetown University Law Center.

articles.title: Foreign citizen beaten to death during march in South Africa as anti-immigrant tensions flare
articles.summary: A foreign citizen was beaten to death by a group of around 50 people during a protest march in South Africa’s east coast city of Durban, police said Thursday, as anti-immigrant tensions continue to flare in Africa’s most advanced economy.
articles.body: A foreign citizen was beaten to death by a group of around 50 people during a protest march in South Africa’s east coast city of Durban, police said Thursday, as anti-immigrant tensions continue to flare in Africa’s most advanced economy. Police said the group approached the man, who was standing at the side of a road during a march through the streets of Durban’s city center, and assaulted him. Police did not immediately give the man’s nationality or details on what the march was related to. They said the victim was in his 30s or early 40s, and they were still trying to identify suspects in the attack. South Africa has struggled with months of anti-immigration tensions. Marches calling for government action against migrants in the country illegally have sometimes spilled over into violence. Nigeria, Mozambique, Malawi and other countries have said some of their citizens have been killed in xenophobic attacks linked to the anti-immigration protests. South African authorities have disputed some of those claims and said some deaths were related to criminal activity and not the protests. Tens of thousands of migrants have left South Africa in recent months in one of the biggest mass exoduses in years. Many cite the threat of violence from angry locals, though the government also said that many were deported for not having the proper documents to be in South Africa. As Africa’s biggest economy, South Africa attracts migrants from many nations on the continent, but that has sometimes brought tensions within communities because of the country’s extremely high unemployment rate and overburdened public services. Durban, South Africa’s third-biggest city of nearly four million people, has become a hotspot for the anti-immigrant tensions that have surged this year. In June, thousands of migrants mainly from Malawi gathered at a park in the city seeking to be repatriated to their home country. They claimed they were fleeing threats of violence after a protest group demanded undocumented migrants leave South Africa by June 30. The camp of migrants seeking to leave grew so quickly that authorities had to build more temporary accommodation centers to handle the numbers. This month, cars were torched and shops were looted in the Johannesburg township of Soweto after a court ruling made it easier for foreign citizens to claim asylum in South Africa, leading to many making applications at government buildings and sparking a reaction from locals. South African President Cyril Ramaphosa has denounced violence related to immigration but has also acknowledged failures in the border control system over the years that have allowed migrants to travel to and stay in South Africa without documentation. South Africa’s official government figures show there are around 2.4 million foreign nationals among the country’s population of 62 million, but protesters say there are many more in South Africa without documentation who haven’t been counted.

articles.title: Strong 7-magnitude earthquake strikes China’s Tibet region
articles.summary: A strong magnitude 7 earthquake struck China’s Tibet at 10.30 p.m. local time on Thursday, according to the United States Geological Survey (USGS).
articles.body: A strong magnitude 7 earthquake struck China’s Tibet at 10.30 p.m. local time on Thursday, according to the United States Geological Survey (USGS). The epicenter was 183 kilometers East-Northeast of the city of Nagqu in western China’s Tibet Autonomous Region, USGS data shows. The scope of the damage is currently unclear. China is no stranger to powerful quakes, especially in southwestern parts of the country where the Eurasian tectonic plate meets the Indian plate, a dramatic collision that creates the mighty Himalayas and the vast Tibetan plateau. The last comparably-strong earthquake to rock China occurred in January 2024, when a 7.1-magnitude quake hit a mountainous and remote part of China’s far western Xinjiang region, killing three people and injuring scores more. In December 2023, over one hundred people were killed when an earthquake hit China’s Jishishan county in Gansu province, northwest China, making it the country’s deadliest in nearly a decade. This is a developing story and will be updated.

articles.title: Emergency powers planned to protect UK's undersea cables
articles.summary: Ministers are set to gain powers over telecoms companies during national security emergencies.
articles.body:
The government has outlined new measures to protect the UK's undersea internet cables amid increased fears of Russian interference.

Ministers are set to gain powers to order telecom companies to remove or disable services during national security emergencies, as well as granting officials access to sites including cable landing stations.

The government has also outlined plans for stronger criminal penalties for those convicted of tampering with either undersea internet cables or energy pipelines.

The new powers would be backed up with prison sentences of up to 14 years for intentional conduct, 10 years for reckless conduct and two years for grossly negligent conduct, alongside unlimited fines.

It comes amid growing fears of suspicious activity in UK waters, and concerns that legal powers over the network have not kept pace with its growing importance to national security.

An extensive network of undersea cables and pipelines owned and operated primarily by the private sector are thought to carry almost all the UK's international data traffic and three-quarters of its gas supplies.

The growing importance of undersea infrastructure prompted a parliamentary report last year to warn of security vulnerabilities in areas including transport and supply chains, financial services and payment systems.

The UK and its Nato allies are concerned about the risk Russia poses to offshore infrastructure.

In April, the government accused Russian submarines of conducting a covert operation over cables and pipelines in waters north of the UK.

The UK has also accused Russia of mapping undersea infrastructure using spy ships. Last year, it revealed the Royal Navy had tracked one such suspected ship, the Yantar, after it passed near UK waters.

Russia has denied the claims, and accused the UK of stirring up tensions through "anti-Russian alarmism".

In a policy paper on Thursday, the government said it currently lacked emergency powers to deal with incidents affecting undersea infrastructure.

It added there were currently no equivalent powers to measures that allow intervention in the water and air traffic sectors, whilst broader powers for national emergencies could prove too slow to exercise during a crisis.

It is now proposing new powers that would allow it to force telecoms companies to hand over information or modify or disable services in connection with specific threats or incidents.

The changes will require new legislation, to be set out after a consultation with industry closing in January.

Companies that refused to comply with the orders could be fined up to £17m or 10% of global turnover. The orders would typically be published, but could be made secret on national security grounds, it added.

The proposed powers are not intended to apply to companies operating energy infrastructure, although the document added that new powers in this area were being considered separately.

Ministers said they hoped the new powers would apply across the "full extent" of undersea services, including outside the UK's territorial waters, which extend up to 12 nautical miles from the coast.

However, the document concedes this is likely to require co-ordination with other countries, adding that the government was considering how its proposals compare to equivalent regimes internationally.

It was also uncertain that existing laws on undersea infrastructure, dating from the Victorian period and designed for telegraphic cables, could be used for breaches of modern fibre-optic cables, the document added.

articles.title: Durban attack: Crowd of 50 beats foreigner to death in South Africa
articles.summary: The attack on the unidentified victim follows a wave of anti-migrants protests in South Africa this year.
articles.body:
A foreign national has been beaten to death by a crowd of about 50 people in Durban, South Africa, police say.

According to police, the unidentified man, believed to be in his late 30s or early 40s, was first approached by two men by the roadside before being assaulted by a larger group. He was pronounced dead at the scene.

Police have launched an investigation into the murder, with the motive yet to be established.

The killing follows a wave of protests against immigrants in South Africa this year, some of which have turned violent. Earlier this month, shops and cars were set on fire in Durban, as well as Soweto, near Johannesburg.

Provincial police spokesperson Robert Netshiunda told the BBC they cannot speculate on the motive for the killing in Durban and that more information would be shared once verified.

'We have to prioritise South Africans': Anti-migrant movement blocks foreigners from healthcare

The uniformed group targeting foreigners in South Africa

The government has urged the demonstrators to act peacefully, while also accepting the need for immigration reforms. It says tens of thousands of foreign nationals have been deported or repatriated since it launched a crackdown earlier this year.

One of the groups behind the protests, March and March, had initially set a deadline of 30 June for all undocumented migrants to leave South Africa.

Several protests were held ahead of that deadline, with reports of attacks on people from other African countries.

These prompted several countries, including Zimbabwe, Nigeria and Ghana, to take steps to repatriate their citizens amid fears of further violence.

Nigeria accused South African authorities of responsibility for the deaths of two of its citizens that month.

Ghana also confirmed the death of a citizen, Bashiru Isak, a father of three who was fatally shot in Cape Town during demonstrations targeting foreign nationals.

His death led to a diplomatic row with South Africa, which said the scale of the violence had been exaggerated.

One of the leaders of the March and March movement, Jacinta Ngobese-Zuma, denied that she was xenophobic.

"We can't be living with these people for so many years and now when we say it is too much, it is enough, we are told that we are xenophobic," she told the BBC's Focus on Africa programme.

South Africa has struggled with xenophobic attacks for nearly two decades. In 2008, more than 60 people were killed and tens of thousands displaced during widespread attacks on foreign nationals.

The latest unrest comes against a backdrop of widespread poverty, deep inequality and unemployment affecting roughly a third of the workforce.

Migrants are frequently accused of taking jobs, contributing to crime and placing pressure on public services, although researchers say such sweeping claims are not supported by evidence.

Despite its economic difficulties, South Africa remains one of the continent's main destinations for migrants seeking employment, safety and better opportunities.
