articles.title: Trump ordered to answer questions under oath in BBC lawsuit
articles.summary: Trump is suing the BBC over an episode of Panorama that edited together two different sections of a speech he gave in 2021.
articles.body:
A US judge has ordered President Donald Trump to answer questions under oath in his defamation lawsuit against the BBC by 11 December.

Trump is suing the BBC over an episode of Panorama that edited together two different sections of a speech he gave before the riot at the US Capitol in 2021.

Charles Tobin, a lawyer representing the BBC, said in court that "we still haven't been able to depose the plaintiff" with two months left in the discovery period.

Trump cancelled a previous deposition on 16 October, citing "matters of national importance" while he was campaigning in Georgia.

In US law, a deposition is an out-of-court statement made under oath in response to questions, which is recorded for use in later proceedings.

The judge in the case, US Magistrate Judge Enjoliqué Lett, said that Trump must sit for the deposition by 11 December, unless the discovery period is extended.

Last week, attorneys asked that Lett compel Trump to face deposition after the last scheduled meeting did not take place.

On that day, Trump attended a midterms campaign rally in Dalton, Georgia and a fundraiser at his property in Mar-a-Lago in Florida.

In a separate filing on Wednesday, Trump's lawyers said that the president could appear for the interview between 11 and 22 January next year, and claimed that the BBC was "wrong to claim that President Trump is avoiding his deposition in this action."

Trump's lawsuit - filed in Florida - accuses the BBC of "intentionally, maliciously, and deceptively doctoring" the speech he gave outside the Capitol on 6 January 2021.

The BBC apologised for the error and said that the broadcast gave "the mistaken impression that President Trump made a direct call for violent action".

The broadcaster has since asked that the court dismiss the lawsuit, arguing that the programme does not meet the legal criteria for defamation and was not available in the US.

In July, Trump's lawyers conceded that they had no evidence that the documentary was available in the US on the BBC's BritBox subscription service - as they originally claimed - or on the BBC's website, BBC select or through US broadcasters.

Trump ultimately agreed to drop the lawsuit against BBC Studios, its commercial arm, after the BBC argued that it had "no role in creating or producing the documentary.

Typically, depositions take place in a lawyer's office - rather than a courtroom - without a judge physically present.

Depositions, however, carry legal weight and take place under oath. They are recorded verbatim by a court reporter, and the transcripts can later be used as evidence during trials.

articles.title: Trump says he called Google’s CEO to rename the Atlantic Ocean
articles.summary: President Trump said Wednesday he asked Google CEO Sundar Pichai to rename the Atlantic Ocean on the company’s Google Maps application, a request the tech executive denied. “We seriously looked at the Atlantic Ocean,” Trump said during a rally in Clemson, S.C. The president then praised Google Maps for changing the respective names of the…
articles.body:
President Trump said Wednesday he asked Google CEO Sundar Pichai to rename the Atlantic Ocean on the company’s Google Maps application, a request the tech executive denied.

“We seriously looked at the Atlantic Ocean,” Trump said during a rally in Clemson, S.C.

The president then praised Google Maps for changing the respective names of the Gulf of Mexico and Lake Ontario to “Gulf of America” and “Lake America,” after he signed executive orders to rename the bodies of water.

The updated names are on display for users of the app in the U.S. Users in Canada still see “Lake Ontario,” while those outside the two countries see both names.

Trump added he spoke to Pichai, whom he called a “brilliant guy,” about renaming the Atlantic Ocean.

“I said, ‘Sundar, I’m thinking of the Atlantic Ocean, can you handle it?’” the president said of their conversation.

But Pichai pushed back on Trump’s request, saying, “No, no, no. This time I’m not doing it,” the president recalled, chuckling.

Pichai added, “They cover … a lot of countries, please don’t ask us to do that,” according to Trump.

The president then noted he will “probably pass” on attempting to rename the Atlantic Ocean, the second-largest of the world’s five oceans.

Trump did not say what he intended to rename the Atlantic Ocean. The Hill has reached out to the White House and Google for comment.

The president signed an order to rename the Gulf of Mexico to the Gulf of America on his first day back in office.

In August, Trump signed an order to rename Lake Ontario , one of the five Great Lakes, to Lake America amid an ongoing trade dispute with Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney.

The president on Monday urged New Mexico to change its name to “New America,” which garnered pushback from Democratic leaders in the state.

“We are New Mexicans,” Sen. Ben Ray Luján (D-N.M.) wrote Monday on social platform X.

“We’re proud of our name, proud of our home, and we’re keeping both,” he added. “Long after Donald Trump is out of office, we’ll still be New Mexico.”

articles.title: Woman loses Rs 8.8L to fake astrologers on social media
articles.summary: Belagavi woman duped of Rs 8.86 lakh by fake Instagram astrologers promising marriage help; paid via UPI/RTGS after WhatsApp chats. Case under probe.
articles.body: Belagavi: A young woman from Belagavi district was allegedly cheated of Rs 8.8 lakh by fraudsters posing as astrologers on Instagram and promising to resolve her personal problems and help her find a suitable groom.According to a complaint filed with Belagavi District Cyber Crime police, the woman found an Instagram account named ‘Pandit M.N. Rao’ on July 3. The profile claimed to offer astrological guidance and asked people facing personal difficulties to contact a listed mobile number.Seeking advice about her marriage prospects, she contacted the number. The alleged astrologer then communicated with her through WhatsApp, shared a list of purported astrological issues and sought her photograph for a detailed horoscope analysis.The fraudsters allegedly claimed they could remove obstacles affecting her life, perform remedial rituals and help her find a suitable partner. They contacted her from two other mobile numbers and repeatedly persuaded her to pay for astrological remedies and services.Police said the accused gradually gained her trust by promising positive changes in her personal life and marriage prospects. She subsequently transferred Rs 8,86,401 from her Bank of Baroda account through PhonePe, Google Pay and RTGS transactions in multiple stages.After the promised results failed to materialise, the woman realised she had been cheated and approached Cyber Crime Police.Police registered a case and are investigating to trace the accused and recover the money. articles.title: Congress must close this tariff loophole
articles.summary: Can Congress meaningfully constrain presidential tariff authority when an older, less restrictive statute offers an alternative route to achieve the same goal?
articles.body:
President Trump’s most recent tariffs are headed to court. On Oct. 20, the Liberty Justice Center filed a lawsuit on behalf of Gellert Global Group, an American food importer, challenging his use of Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930 to impose tariffs on Canadian goods.

The case exposes a loophole in U.S. trade law that the courts may not be able to close, but that Congress can no longer afford to ignore.

One of the complaint’s main arguments is that Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974 effectively replaced Section 338. That will be a difficult legal argument to win. But it raises a compelling question: Can Congress meaningfully constrain presidential tariff authority when an older, less restrictive statute offers an alternative route to achieve the same goal?

Section 338 addresses discrimination against American commerce. It authorizes additional duties of up to 50 percent when a foreign country subjects U.S. products or commerce to specified forms of unequal treatment. Those duties must “ offset ” the resulting burden or disadvantage.

Section 301 casts a wider net. It addresses foreign practices that are unreasonable, unjustifiable or discriminatory that burden or restrict U.S. commerce. Discrimination is one form of unfair trade practice, but Section 301 reaches considerably further.

The statutes are therefore not interchangeable. Yet they overlap when foreign discrimination becomes the basis for American retaliation. That’s what is happening with the Canada tariffs.

Congress wrote Section 301 with safeguards. The U.S. Trade Representative generally must investigate the conduct at issue, consult with the foreign government, invite public comment, provide opportunities for hearings and make findings within statutory deadlines. Certain remedies must be equivalent in value to the burden imposed, and enforcement actions face periodic review.

Section 338 has limits as well, including requirements concerning discrimination, offsetting duties and a waiting period. But it lacks Section 301’s comparable investigation, consultation, public participation and review procedures.

This creates a loophole. Why would the president ever proceed under Section 301, with its procedural obligations, if Section 338 produces the same outcome with fewer fetters?

The president i nvoked Section 338 to respond to Canadian measures affecting American alcohol, dairy products and automobiles. Each proclamation imposed the statutory maximum tariff of 50 percent.

The lawsuit challenges whether these measures constitute discrimination within the meaning of Section 338, as well as the administration’s failure to explain how identical 50 percent duties offset the different burdens identified. A court may find that the administration exceeded Section 338’s limits.

But the complaint goes a step further, arguing that Congress effectively displaced Section 338 when it established the more comprehensive Section 301 framework.

That argument faces long odds. Courts strongly disfavor implied repeals. Congress never expressly repealed Section 338, and the statutes address different, albeit overlapping, categories of foreign conduct. The mere existence of a newer, more elaborate remedy does not necessarily supplant an older one. The courts may therefore conclude that both statutes remain available.

But that is precisely the problem that Congress must address.

A court may curtail the administration’s use of Section 338 in this case, but it is unlikely to invalidate the statute itself. That would leave presidents with two routes for responding to certain discriminatory foreign trade practices: one governed by Section 301’s extensive procedural safeguards, the other subject to far fewer.

Congress has several options. It could repeal Section 338, narrow its application or require comparable safeguards when the two statutes overlap. Alternatively, it could clarify which authority governs particular forms of discrimination. Each approach would strike a different balance between presidential flexibility and congressional oversight.

What Congress must not do is leave this balance unresolved.

The courts can enforce limits on Section 338. They are unlikely to resolve the broader relationship between the two statutes through implied repeal. That leaves Congress with a choice: reconcile the authorities or accept that Section 301’s safeguards can sometimes be circumvented.

Congress spent decades placing limits on presidential trade retaliation, but Section 338 offers a potential way around them. Unless lawmakers reconcile the two statutes, presidents may be free to circumvent the safeguards Congress deliberately built into Section 301.

Marc L. Busch is the Karl F. Landegger Professor of International Business Diplomacy at the Walsh School of Foreign Service, Georgetown University.

articles.title: Fox News host: Russians ‘must be laughing their heads off’ over Witkoff ‘humanitarian’ remark
articles.summary: Fox News host Brian Kilmeade posted a video clip of himself on the social platform X criticizing special envoy Steve Witkoff’s comment calling Russian President Vladimir Putin “a humanitarian.” “The Russians must be laughing their heads off,” Kilmeade said in the video. “That just makes you look naïve. A humanitarian? This guy kills his opponents,…
articles.body:
Fox News host Brian Kilmeade posted a video clip of himself on the social platform X criticizing special envoy Steve Witkoff’s comment calling Russian President Vladimir Putin “a humanitarian.”

“The Russians must be laughing their heads off,” Kilmeade said in the video.

“That just makes you look naïve. A humanitarian? This guy kills his opponents, he arrests journalists … ladies and gentlemen, anyone listening, if you see Vladimir Putin, do not call him a humanitarian,” he continued.

Kilmeade’s remarks are in regard to what Witkoff said to Putin in St. Petersburg, Russia following the release of Stephen Hubbard on Wednesday.

“You talk so much about my president, President Trump, being a humanitarian,” Witkoff said to Putin. “You are a humanitarian also, sir, and I salute that.”

Hubbard was released Wednesday and has returned to the U.S. after being detained in Russia for nearly four years. He arrived at Lackland Air Force Base in San Antonio early Thursday morning. Trump said he personally asked the Russian president to release Hubbard in a phone call, and Witkoff traveled to Russia to secure his release.

Witkoff’s remarks sparked backlash across the board with multiple Republicans, including Sen. Thom Tillis (N.C.), criticizing his comment.

“Look up the definition of ‘humanitarian.’ What an embarrassing and outrageous thing to say,” Tillis wrote X. “You should go back to Ukraine and ask the families of the children Putin has kidnapped and murdered whether they agree your friend Putin is a ‘humanitarian.’”
